features.text: The patient is 58 years old and female.
The patient has been experiencing shortness of breath that has been worsening over the weekend and is currently severe, making it difficult to walk down the street.
The patient has pain when swallowing, which is constant every time she swallows, regardless of what she eats or drinks, and is located in the chest area.
The patient does not have chest pain.
The patient has been experiencing weight loss and fatigue.
The patient is undergoing chemotherapy with a combination of cisplatin and etoposide.
The patient experienced nausea and fatigue from chemotherapy, but the Zofran prescribed helped with the nausea.
The patient has no significant past medical history other than lung cancer.
The patient has no allergies.
The patient has no history of surgeries.
The patient is unaware of any family history of cancer or respiratory conditions.
The patient's vital signs are normal, and her pulse ox is okay.
The patient's doctor did not find any swollen lymph nodes in her neck.
The patient's heart sounds were normal.
The patient's doctor heard crackles in her lungs, which may be due to fluid.
The patient has redness on her chest, possibly from radiation.
The patient does not have swelling in her legs.
The patient's chest X-ray showed mild radiation pneumonitis, which is inflammation of the lungs from radiation treatment.
The patient's doctor mentioned there might be some fluid in her lungs, but no pleural effusion was specifically identified.
The patient's dysphagia has worsened since the start of radiation therapy.
The patient has not undergone an endoscopic evaluation of the esophagus to confirm esophagitis or other structural abnormalities.
The patient has not undergone any esophageal imaging studies, such as a barium swallow or esophagram.
The patient has not experienced any changes in her voice, such as hoarseness, or difficulty breathing when lying down.
The patient hopes that lidocaine will help with the pain when swallowing.
